column4: Yes. I looked at PO 4952, a high-criticality pharmacy item from Supplier 053. The Management Review page said it was flagged for two reasons: a delivery delay could add up to about 654 more units of unmet demand, and the item is already short even if it arrives on time (8 stockout days and about 745 unmet units at baseline). The delay scenarios showed things getting worse fast. A 3-day delay adds about 280 short units and $132 in emergency premium, 5 days adds about 467 units and $219, and 7 days adds about 654 units and $307. Since it’s a critical item that’s already running short, I’d recommend expediting the order or lining up a backup supplier now instead of waiting to see if it’s late. I’d record that decision under the Decision Records tab in the Management section. The tool made the risk pretty clear, but it doesn’t suggest an action itself, so the final call is still up to the manager.
column8: Some of the wording was hard to follow without a technical background. Phrases like “stored point-in-time DSS assessments,” “retrospective what-if,” “unresolved screening,” and the “MR-01/MR-02 consistency check” didn’t really mean anything to me at first, and I had to read them a few times to figure out what they were saying. The emergency premium was also a little confusing. I first assumed it was the total cost of fixing the shortage, until I saw the small note saying it’s only the extra unit-price cost. The main table was a lot to take in too, since it has 453 POs and small text, so it took me a minute to find the order I was looking at. It also wasn’t obvious at first that the reasons for the flag and the place to record a decision were in a separate Management section, so I had to click around to find them.
column9: I’d add short plain-language explanations next to the technical terms, either as a hover tooltip or a one-line description under each section. For example, “MR-01” could just say “this order could run short if delivery is late,” and the emergency premium could say upfront that it’s the extra cost per unit, not the total cost. That would make the tool much easier for a manager without a technical background to use, and they wouldn’t have to guess what each label means before making a decision.
